arXiv:1503.03465v8 [cs.DS] 04 Nov 2015

Faster 64-bit universal hashing using carry-less multiplications

Daniel Lemire    Owen Kaser Affiliation: LICEF Research Center, TELUQ, Université du Québec
Montreal, QC Canada E-mail: lemire@gmail.com Affiliation: Dept. of CSAS, University of New Brunswick, Saint John
Saint John, NB Canada E-mail: o.kaser@computer.org
Abstract

Intel and AMD support the Carry-less Multiplication (CLMUL) instruction set in their x64 processors. We use CLMUL to implement an almost universal 64-bit hash family (CLHASH). We compare this new family with what might be the fastest almost universal family on x64 processors (VHASH). We find that CLHASH is at least 60 %60\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} faster. We also compare CLHASH with a popular hash function designed for speed (Google’s CityHash). We find that CLHASH is 40 %40\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} faster than CityHash on inputs larger than 64 bytes and just as fast otherwise.

Keywords: 
Universal hashing, Carry-less multiplication, Finite field arithmetic

1 Introduction

Hashing is the fundamental operation of mapping data objects to fixed-size hash values. For example, all objects in the Java programming language can be hashed to 32-bit integers. Many algorithms and data structures rely on hashing: e.g., authentication codes, Bloom filters and hash tables. We typically assume that given two data objects, the probability that they have the same hash value (called a collision) is low. When this assumption fails, adversaries can negatively impact the performance of these data structures or even create denial-of-service attacks. To mitigate such problems, we can pick hash functions at random (henceforth called random hashing).

Random hashing is standard in Ruby, Python and Perl. It is allowed explicitly in Java and C++11. There are many fast random hash families — e.g., MurmurHash, Google’s CityHash [35], SipHash [3] and VHASH [12]. Cryptographers have also designed fast hash families with strong theoretical guarantees [6, 18, 24]. However, much of this work predates the introduction of the CLMUL instruction set in commodity x86 processors. Intel and AMD added CLMUL and its pclmulqdq instruction to their processors to accelerate some common cryptographic operations. Although the pclmulqdq instruction first became available in 2010, its high cost in terms of CPU cycles — specifically an 8-cycle throughput on pre-Haswell Intel microarchitectures and a 7-cycle throughput on pre-Jaguar AMD microarchitectures — limited its usefulness outside of cryptography. However, the throughput of the instruction on the newer Haswell architecture is down to 2 cycles, even though it remains a high latency operation (7 cycles) [16, 21].11 1 The low-power AMD Jaguar microarchitecture does even better with a throughput of 1 cycle and a latency of 3 cycles. See Table 1. Our main contribution is to show that the pclmulqdq instruction can be used to produce a 64-bit string hash family that is faster than known approaches while offering stronger theoretical guarantees.

2 Random Hashing

In random hashing, we pick a hash function at random from some family, whereas an adversary might pick the data inputs. We want distinct objects to be unlikely to hash to the same value. That is, we want a low collision probability.

We consider hash functions from XX to [0,2L)[0,2^{L}). An LL-bit family is universal [10, 11] if the probability of a collision is no more than 2−L2^{-L}. That is, it is universal if

P⁡(h⁡(x)=h⁡(x′))≤2−L\displaystyle P\left(h(x)=h(x^{\prime})\right)\leq 2^{-L}

for any fixed x,x′∈Xx,x^{\prime}\in X such that x≠x′x\neq x^{\prime}, given that we pick hh at random from the family. It is ϵ\epsilon-almost universal [36] (also written ϵ\epsilon-AU) if the probability of a collision is bounded by ϵ\epsilon. I.e., P⁡(h⁡(x)=h⁡(x′))≤ϵP\left(h(x)=h(x^{\prime})\right)\leq\epsilon, for any x,x′∈Xx,x^{\prime}\in X such that x≠x′x\neq x^{\prime}. (See Table 2.)

2.1 Safely Reducing Hash Values

Almost universality can be insufficient to prevent frequent collisions since a given algorithm might only use the first few bits of the hash values. Consider hash tables. A hash table might use as a key only the first bb bits of the hash values when its capacity is 2b2^{b}. Yet even if a hash family is ϵ\epsilon-almost universal, it could still have a high collision probability on the first few bits.

For example, take any 3232-bit universal family ℋ\mathcal{H}, and derive the new 6464-bit 1/2321/2^{32}-almost universal 6464-bit family by taking the functions from ℋ\mathcal{H} and multiplying them by 2322^{32}: h′​(x)=h⁡(x)×232h^{\prime}(x)=h(x)\times 2^{32}. Clearly, all functions from this new family collide with probability 1 on the first 32 bits, even though the collision probability on the full hash values is low (1/2321/2^{32}). Using the first bits of these hash functions could have disastrous consequences in the implementation of a hash table.

Therefore, we consider stronger forms of universality.

  • •

    A family is Δ\Delta-universal [37, 14] if

    P⁡(h⁡(x)=h⁡(x′)+cmod2L)≤2−L\displaystyle P(h(x)=h(x^{\prime})+c\bmod 2^{L})\leq 2^{-L}

    for any constant cc and any x,x′∈Xx,x^{\prime}\in X such that x≠x′x\neq x^{\prime}. It is ϵ\epsilon-almost Δ\Delta-universal if P⁡(h⁡(x)=h⁡(x′)+cmod2L≤ϵCLOSEP(h(x)=h(x^{\prime})+c\bmod 2^{L}\leq\epsilon for any constant cc and any x,x′∈Xx,x^{\prime}\in X such that x≠x′x\neq x^{\prime}.

  • •

    A family is ϵ\epsilon-almost XOR-universal if

    P⁡(h⁡(x)=h⁡(x′)⊕c)≤ϵ\displaystyle P\left(h(x)=h(x^{\prime})\oplus c\right)\leq\epsilon

    for any integer constant c∈[0,2L)c\in[0,2^{L}) and any x,x′∈Xx,x^{\prime}\in X such that x≠x′x\neq x^{\prime} (where ⊕\oplus is the bitwise XOR). A family that is 1/2L1/2^{L}-almost XOR-universal is said to be XOR-universal [37].

Given an ϵ\epsilon-almost Δ\Delta-universal family ℋ\mathcal{H} of hash functions h:X→[0,2L)h:X\to[0,2^{L}), the family of hash functions

{h(x)mod2L′|h∈ℋ}\displaystyle\{h(x)\bmod 2^{L^{\prime}}\>\lvert\>h\in\mathcal{H}\}

from XX to [0,2L′)[0,2^{L^{\prime}}) is 2L−L′×ϵ2^{L-L^{\prime}}\times\epsilon-almost Δ\Delta-universal [12]. The next lemma shows that a similar result applies to almost XOR-almost universal families.

Lemma 1

Given an ϵ\epsilon-almost XOR-universal family ℋ\mathcal{H} of hash functions h:X→[0,2L)h:X\to[0,2^{L}) and any positive integer L′<LL^{\prime}<L, the family of hash functions {h(x)mod2L′|h∈ℋ}\{h(x)\bmod 2^{L^{\prime}}\>\lvert\>h\in\mathcal{H}\} from XX to [0,2L′)[0,2^{L^{\prime}}) is 2L−L′×ϵ2^{L-L^{\prime}}\times\epsilon-almost XOR-universal.

Proof

For any integer constant c∈[0,2L)c\in[0,2^{L}), consider the equation h⁡(x)=(h⁡(x′)⊕c)mod2L′h(x)=(h(x^{\prime})\oplus c)\bmod 2^{L^{\prime}} for x≠x′x\neq x^{\prime} with hh picked from ℋ\mathcal{H}. Pick any positive integer L′<LL^{\prime}<L. We have

P⁡(CLOSE\displaystyle P( OPENh⁡(x)=(h⁡(x′)⊕cmod2L′))\displaystyle h(x)=(h(x^{\prime})\oplus c\mod 2^{L^{\prime}}))
=∑z|zmod2L′=0P(h(x)=h(x′)⊕c⊕z)\displaystyle=\sum_{z\>\lvert\>z\bmod 2^{L^{\prime}}=0}P(h(x)=h(x^{\prime})\oplus c\oplus z)

where the sum is over 2L−L′2^{L-L^{\prime}} distinct zz values. Because ℋ\mathcal{H} is ϵ\epsilon-almost XOR-universal, we have that P⁡(h⁡(x)=h⁡(x′)⊕c⊕z)≤ϵP(h(x)=h(x^{\prime})\oplus c\oplus z)\leq\epsilon for any cc and any zz. Thus, we have that P⁡(h⁡(x)=h⁡(x′)⊕cmod2L′)≤2L−L′​ϵP(h(x)=h(x^{\prime})\oplus c\mod 2^{L^{\prime}})\leq 2^{L-L^{\prime}}\epsilon, showing the result.

It follows from Lemma 1 that if a family is XOR-universal, then its modular reductions are XOR-universal as well.

As a straightforward extension of this lemma, we could show that when picking any L′L^{\prime} bits (not only the least significant), the result is 2L−L′×ϵ2^{L-L^{\prime}}\times\epsilon-almost XOR-universal.

2.2 Composition

It can be useful to combine different hash families to create new ones. For example, it is common to compose hash families. When composing hash functions (h=g∘fh=g\circ f), the universality degrades linearly: if gg is picked from an ϵg\epsilon_{g}-almost universal family and ff is picked (independently) from an ϵf\epsilon_{f}-almost universal family, the result is ϵg+ϵf\epsilon_{g}+\epsilon_{f}-almost universal [36].

We sketch the proof. For x≠x′x\neq x^{\prime}, we have that g⁡(f⁡(x))=g⁡(f⁡(x′))g(f(x))=g(f(x^{\prime})) collides if f​(x)=f′​(x)f(x)=f^{\prime}(x). This occurs with probability at most ϵf\epsilon_{f} since ff is picked from an ϵf\epsilon_{f}-almost universal family. If not, they collide if g⁡(y)=g⁡(y′)g(y)=g(y^{\prime}) where y=f⁡(x)y=f(x) and y′=f⁡(x′)y^{\prime}=f(x^{\prime}), with probability bounded by ϵg\epsilon_{g}. Thus, we have bounded the collision probability by ϵf+(1−ϵf)​ϵg≤ϵf+ϵg\epsilon_{f}+(1-\epsilon_{f})\epsilon_{g}\leq\epsilon_{f}+\epsilon_{g}, establishing the result.

By extension, we can show that if gg is picked from an ϵg\epsilon_{g}-almost XOR-universal family, then the composed result (h=g∘fh=g\circ f) is going to be ϵg+ϵf\epsilon_{g}+\epsilon_{f}-almost XOR-universal. It is not required for ff to be almost XOR-universal.

2.3 Hashing Tuples

If we have universal hash functions from XX to [0,2L)[0,2^{L}), then we can construct hash functions from XmX^{m} to [0,2L)m[0,2^{L})^{m} while preserving universality. The construction is straightforward: h′​(x1,x2,…,xm)=(h⁡(x1),h⁡(x2),…,h⁡(xm))h^{\prime}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{m})=(h(x_{1}),h(x_{2}),\ldots,h(x_{m})). If hh is picked from an ϵ\epsilon-almost universal family, then the result is ϵ\epsilon-almost universal. This is true even though a single hh is picked and reused mm times.

Lemma 2

Consider an ϵ\epsilon-almost universal family ℋ\mathcal{H} from XX to [0,2L)[0,2^{L}). Then consider the family of functions ℋ′\mathcal{H}^{\prime} of the form h′​(x1,x2,…,xm)=(h⁡(x1),h⁡(x2),…,h⁡(xm))h^{\prime}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{m})=(h(x_{1}),h(x_{2}),\ldots,h(x_{m})) from XmX^{m} to [0,2L)m[0,2^{L})^{m}, where hh is in ℋ\mathcal{H}. Family ℋ′\mathcal{H}^{\prime} is ϵ\epsilon-almost universal.

The proof is not difficult. Consider two distinct values from XmX^{m}, x1,x2,…,xmx_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{m} and x1′,x2′,…,xm′x^{\prime}_{1},x^{\prime}_{2},\ldots,x^{\prime}_{m}. Because the tuples are distinct, they must differ in at least one component: xi≠xi′x_{i}\neq x^{\prime}_{i}. It follows that h′​(x1,x2,…,xm)h^{\prime}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{m}) and h′​(x1′,x2′,…,xm′)h^{\prime}(x^{\prime}_{1},x^{\prime}_{2},\ldots,x^{\prime}_{m}) collide with probability at most P⁡(h⁡(xi)=h⁡(xi′))≤ϵP(h(x_{i})=h(x^{\prime}_{i}))\leq\epsilon, showing the result.

2.4 Variable-Length Hashing From Fixed-Length Hashing

Suppose that we are given a family ℋ\mathcal{H} of hash functions that is XOR universal over fixed-length strings. That is, we have that P⁡(h⁡(s)=h⁡(s′)⊕c)≤1/2LP\left(h(s)=h(s^{\prime})\oplus c\right)\leq 1/2^{L} if the length of ss is the same as the length of s′s^{\prime} (|s|=|s′||s|=|s^{\prime}|). We can create a new family that is XOR universal over variable-length strings by introducing a hash family on string lengths. Let 𝒢\mathcal{G} be a family of XOR universal hash functions gg over length values. Consider the new family of hash functions of the form h⁡(s)⊕g⁡(|s|)h(s)\oplus g(|s|) where h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H} and g∈𝒢g\in\mathcal{G}. Let us consider two distinct strings ss and s′s^{\prime}. There are two cases to consider.

  • •

    If ss and s′s^{\prime} have the same length so that g⁡(|s|)=g⁡(|s′|)g(|s|)=g(|s^{\prime}|) then we have XOR universality since

    P⁡(h⁡(s)⊕g⁡(|s|)=h⁡(s′)⊕g⁡(|s′|)⊕c)\displaystyle P\left(h(s)\oplus g(|s|)=h(s^{\prime})\oplus g(|s^{\prime}|)\oplus c\right)
    =P⁡(h⁡(s)=h⁡(s′)⊕c)\displaystyle=P\left(h(s)=h(s^{\prime})\oplus c\right)
    ≤1/2L\displaystyle\leq 1/2^{L}

    where the last inequality follows because h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H}, an XOR universal family over fixed-length strings.

  • •

    If the strings have different lengths (|s|≠|s′||s|\neq|s^{\prime}|), then we again have XOR universality because

    P⁡(h⁡(s)⊕g⁡(|s|)=h⁡(s′)⊕g⁡(|s′|)⊕c)\displaystyle P\left(h(s)\oplus g(|s|)=h(s^{\prime})\oplus g(|s^{\prime}|)\oplus c\right)
    =P⁡(g⁡(|s|)=g⁡(|s′|)⊕(c⊕h⁡(s)⊕h⁡(s′)))\displaystyle=P\left(g(|s|)=g(|s^{\prime}|)\oplus(c\oplus h(s)\oplus h(s^{\prime}))\right)
    =P⁡(g⁡(|s|)=g⁡(|s′|)⊕c′)\displaystyle=P\left(g(|s|)=g(|s^{\prime}|)\oplus c^{\prime}\right)
    ≤1/2L\displaystyle\leq 1/2^{L}

    where we set c′=c⊕h⁡(s)⊕h⁡(s′)c^{\prime}=c\oplus h(s)\oplus h(s^{\prime}), a value independent from |s||s| and |s′||s^{\prime}|. The last inequality follows because gg is taken from a family 𝒢\mathcal{G} that is XOR universal.

Thus the result (h⁡(s)⊕g⁡(|s|)h(s)\oplus g(|s|)) is XOR universal. We can also generalize the analysis. Indeed, if ℋ\mathcal{H} and 𝒢\mathcal{G} are ϵ\epsilon-almost universal, we could show that the result is ϵ\epsilon-almost universal. We have the following lemma.

Lemma 3

Let ℋ\mathcal{H} be an XOR universal family of hash functions over fixed-length strings. Let 𝒢\mathcal{G} be an XOR universal family of hash functions over integer values. We have that the family of hash functions of the form s→h⁡(s)⊕g⁡(|s|)s\to h(s)\oplus g(|s|) where h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H} and g∈𝒢g\in\mathcal{G} is XOR universal over all strings.

Moreover, if ℋ\mathcal{H} and 𝒢\mathcal{G} are merely ϵ\epsilon-almost universal, then the family of hash functions of the form s→h⁡(s)⊕g⁡(|s|)s\to h(s)\oplus g(|s|) is also ϵ\epsilon-almost universal.

2.5 Minimally Randomized Hashing

Many hashing algorithms — for instance, CityHash [35] — rely on a small random seed. The 64-bit version of CityHash takes a 64-bit integer as a seed. Thus, we effectively have a family of 2642^{64} hash functions — one for each possible seed value.

Given such a small family (i.e., given few random bits), we can prove that it must have high collision probabilities. Indeed, consider the set of all strings of mm 64-bit words. There are 264​m2^{64m} such strings.

  • •

    Pick one hash function from the CityHash family. This function hashes every one of the 264​m2^{64m} strings to one of 2642^{64} hash values. By a pigeonhole argument [31], there must be at least one hash value where at least 264​m/264=264​(m−1)2^{64m}/2^{64}=2^{64(m-1)} strings collide.

  • •

    Pick another hash function. Out of the 264​(m−1)2^{64(m-1)} strings colliding when using the first hash function, we must have 264​(m−2)2^{64(m-2)} strings also colliding when using the second hash function.

We can repeat this process m−1m-1 times until we find 2642^{64} strings colliding when using any of these m−1m-1 hash functions. If an adversary picks any two of our 2642^{64} strings and we pick the hash function at random in the whole family of 2642^{64} hash functions, we get a collision with a probability of at least (m−1)/264(m-1)/2^{64}. Thus, while we do not have a strict bound on the collision probability of the CityHash family, we know just from the small size of its seed that it must have a relatively high collision probability for long strings. In contrast, VHASH and our CLHASH (see § 5) use more than 64 random bits and have correspondingly better collision bounds (see Table 4).

3 VHASH

The VHASH family [12, 25] was designed for 64-bit processors. By default, it operates over 64-bit words. Among hash families offering good almost universality for large data inputs, VHASH might be the fastest 64-bit alternative on x64 processors — except for our own proposal (see § 5).

VHASH is ϵ\epsilon-almost Δ\Delta-universal and builds on the 128-bit NH family [12]:

NH⁡(s)=∑i=1l/2(CLOSE\displaystyle\mathrm{NH}(s)=\sum_{i=1}^{l/2}\big( (s2​i−1+k2​i−1mod264)\displaystyle(s_{2i-1}+k_{2i-1}\bmod 2^{64}) (1)
×(s2​i+k2​imod264))mod2128.\displaystyle\times(s_{2i}+k_{2i}\bmod 2^{64})\big)\bmod 2^{128}.

NH is 1/2641/2^{64}-almost Δ\Delta-universal with hash values in [0,2128)[0,2^{128}). Although the NH family is defined only for inputs containing an even number of components, we can extend it to include odd numbers of components by padding the input with a zero component.

We can summarize VHASH (see Algorithm 1) as follows:

  • •

    NH is used to generate a 128-bit hash value for each block of 16 words. The result is 1/2641/2^{64}-almost Δ\Delta-universal on each block.

  • •

    These hash values are mapped to a value in [0,2126)[0,2^{126}) by applying a modular reduction. These reduced hash values are then aggregated with a polynomial hash and finally reduced to a 64-bit value.

In total, the VHASH family is 1/2611/2^{61}-almost Δ\Delta-universal over [0,264−257)[0,2^{64}-257) for input strings of up to 2622^{62} bits (12, Theorem 1).

For long input strings, we expect that much of the running time of VHASH is in the computation of NH on blocks of 16 words. On recent x64 processors, this computation involves 8 multiplications using the mulq instruction (with two 64-bit inputs and two 64-bit outputs). For each group of two consecutive words (sis_{i} and si+1s_{i+1}), we also need two 64-bit additions. To sum all results, we need 7 128-bit additions that can be implemented using two 64-bit additions (addq and adcq). All of these operations have a throughput of at least 1 per cycle on Haswell processors. We can expect NH and, by extension, VHASH to be fast.

VHASH uses only 16 64-bit random integers for the NH family. As in § 2.3, we only need one specific NH function irrespective of the length of the string. VHASH also uses a 128-bit random integer kk and two more 64-bit random integers k1′k^{\prime}_{1} and k2′k^{\prime}_{2}. Thus VHASH uses slightly less than 160 random bytes.

3.1 Random Bits

Nguyen and Roscoe showed that at least log⁡(m/ϵ)\log(m/\epsilon) random bits are required [31],22 2 In the present paper, log⁡n\log n means log2⁡n\log_{2}n. where mm is the maximal string length in bits and ϵ\epsilon is the collision bound. For VHASH, the string length is limited to 2622^{62} bits and the collision bound is ϵ=1/261\epsilon=1/2^{61}. Therefore, for hash families offering the bounds of VHASH, we have that log⁡m/ϵ=log⁡(262×261)=123\log m/\epsilon=\log(2^{62}\times 2^{61})=123 random bits are required.

That is, 16 random bytes are theoretically required to achieve the same collision bound as VHASH while many more are used (160 bytes) This suggests that we might be able to find families using far fewer random bits while maintaining the same good bounds. In fact, it is not difficult to modify VHASH to reduce the use of random bits. It would suffice to reduce the size of the blocks down from 16 words. We could show that it cannot increase the bound on the collision probability by more than 1/2641/2^{64}. However, reducing the size of the blocks has an adverse effect on speed. With large blocks and long strings, most of the input is processed with the NH function before the more expensive polynomial hash function is used. Thus, there is a trade-off between speed and the number of random bits, and VHASH is designed for speed on long strings.

4 Finite Fields

Our proposed hash family (CLHASH, see § 5) works over a binary finite field. For completeness, we review field theory briefly, introducing (classical) results as needed for our purposes.

The real numbers form what is called a field. A field is such that addition and multiplication are associative, commutative and distributive. We also have identity elements (0 for addition and 1 for multiplication). Crucially, all non-zero elements aa have an inverse a−1a^{-1} (which is defined by a×a−1=a−1×a=1a\times a^{-1}=a^{-1}\times a=1).

Finite fields (also called Galois fields) are fields containing a finite number of elements. All finite fields have cardinality pnp^{n} for some prime pp. Up to an algebraic isomorphism (i.e., a one-to-one map preserving addition and multiplication), given a cardinality pnp^{n}, there is only one field (henceforth G​F​(pn)GF(p^{n})). And for any power of a prime, there is a corresponding field.

4.1 Finite Fields of Prime Cardinality

It is easy to create finite fields that have prime cardinality (G​F​(p)GF(p)). Given pp, an instance of G​F​(p)GF(p) is given by the set of integers in [0,p)[0,p) with additions and multiplications completed by a modular reduction:

  • •

    a×G​F​(p)b≡a×bmodpa\times_{GF(p)}b\equiv a\times b\bmod p

  • •

    and a+G​F​(p)b≡a+bmodpa+_{GF(p)}b\equiv a+b\bmod p.

The numbers 0 and 1 are the identity elements. Given an element aa, its additive inverse is p−ap-a.

It is not difficult to check that all non-zero elements have a multiplicative inverse. We review this classical result for completeness. Given a non-zero element aa and two distinct x,x′x,x^{\prime}, we have that a​xmodp≠a​x′modpax\bmod p\neq ax^{\prime}\bmod p because pp is prime. Hence, starting with a fixed non-zero element aa, we have that the set {a​xmodp∣x∈[0,p)}\{ax\bmod p\,\mid\,x\in[0,p)\} has cardinality pp and must contain 1; thus, aa must have a multiplicative inverse.

4.2 Hash Families in a Field

Within a field, we can easily construct hash families having strong theoretical guarantees, as the next lemma illustrates.

Lemma 4

The family of functions of the form

h⁡(x)=a​x\displaystyle h(x)=ax

in a finite field (G​F​(pn)GF(p^{n})) is Δ\Delta-universal, provided that the key aa is picked from all values of the field.

As another example, consider hash functions of the form h⁡(x1,x2,…,xm)=am−1​x1+am−2​x2+⋯+xmh(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{m})=a^{m-1}x_{1}+a^{m-2}x_{2}+\cdots+x_{m} where aa is picked at random (a random input). Such polynomial hash functions can be computed efficiently using Horner’s rule: starting with r=x1r=x_{1}, compute r←a​r+xir\leftarrow ar+x_{i} for i=2,…,mi=2,\ldots,m. Given any two distinct inputs, x1,x2,…,xmx_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{m} and x1′,x2′,…,xm′x^{\prime}_{1},x^{\prime}_{2},\ldots,x^{\prime}_{m}, we have that h⁡(x1,…,xm)−h⁡(x1′,…,xm′)h(x_{1},\ldots,x_{m})-h(x^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,x^{\prime}_{m}) is a non-zero polynomial of degree at most m−1m-1 in aa. By the fundamental theorem of algebra, we have that it is zero for at most m−1m-1 distinct values of aa. Thus we have that the probability of a collision is bounded by (m−1)/pn(m-1)/p^{n} where pnp^{n} is the cardinality of the field. For example, VHASH uses polynomial hashing with p=2127−1p=2^{127}-1 and n=1n=1.

We can further reduce the collision probabilities if we use mm random inputs a1,…,ama_{1},\ldots,a_{m} picked in the field to compute a multilinear function: h⁡(x1,…,xm)=a1​x1+a2​x2+⋯+am​xmh(x_{1},\ldots,x_{m})=a_{1}x_{1}+a_{2}x_{2}+\cdots+a_{m}x_{m}. We have Δ\Delta-universality. Given two distinct inputs, x1,…,xmx_{1},\ldots,x_{m} and x1′,…,xm′x^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,x^{\prime}_{m}, we have that xi≠xi′x_{i}\neq x^{\prime}_{i} for some ii. Thus we have that h⁡(x1,…,xm)=c+h⁡(x1′,…,xm′)h(x_{1},\ldots,x_{m})=c+h(x^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,x^{\prime}_{m}) if and only if ai=(xi−xi′)−1​(c+∑j≠iaj​(xj′−xj))a_{i}=(x_{i}-x^{\prime}_{i})^{-1}(c+\sum_{j\neq i}a_{j}(x^{\prime}_{j}-x_{j})).

If mm is even, we can get the same bound on the collision probability with half the number of multiplications [7, 26, 29]:

h⁡(x1,x2,…,xm)\displaystyle h(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{m})
=(a1+x1)​(a2+x2)+⋯+(am−1+xm−1)​(am+xm).\displaystyle=(a_{1}+x_{1})(a_{2}+x_{2})+\cdots+(a_{m-1}+x_{m-1})(a_{m}+x_{m}).

The argument is similar. Consider that

(xi+ai)​(ai+1+xi+1)−(xi′+ai)​(ai+1+xi+1′)\displaystyle(x_{i}+a_{i})(a_{i+1}+x_{i+1})-(x^{\prime}_{i}+a_{i})(a_{i+1}+x^{\prime}_{i+1})
=ai+1​(xi−xi′)+ai​(xi+1−xi+1′)+xi+1​xi+xi′​xi+1′.\displaystyle=a_{i+1}(x_{i}-x^{\prime}_{i})+a_{i}(x_{i+1}-x^{\prime}_{i+1})+x_{i+1}x_{i}+x^{\prime}_{i}x^{\prime}_{i+1}.

Take two distinct inputs, x1,x2,…,xmx_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{m} and x1′,x2′,…,xm′x^{\prime}_{1},x^{\prime}_{2},\ldots,x^{\prime}_{m}. As before, we have that xi≠xi′x_{i}\neq x^{\prime}_{i} for some ii. Without loss of generality, assume that ii is odd; then we can find a unique solution for ai+1a_{i+1}: to do this, start from h⁡(x1,…,xm)=c+h⁡(x1′,…,xm′)h(x_{1},\ldots,x_{m})=c+h(x^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,x^{\prime}_{m}) and solve for ai+1​(xi−xi′)a_{i+1}(x_{i}-x^{\prime}_{i}) in terms of an expression that does not depend on ai+1a_{i+1}. Then use the fact that xi−xi′x_{i}-x^{\prime}_{i} has an inverse. This shows that the collision probability is bounded by 1/pn1/p^{n} and we have Δ\Delta-universality.

Lemma 5

Given an even number mm, the family of functions of the form

h⁡(x1,x2,…,xm)=\displaystyle h(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{m})= (a1+x1)​(a2+x2)\displaystyle(a_{1}+x_{1})(a_{2}+x_{2})
+(a3+x3)​(a4+x4)\displaystyle+(a_{3}+x_{3})(a_{4}+x_{4})
+⋯\displaystyle+\cdots
+(am−1+xm−1)​(am+xm)\displaystyle+(a_{m-1}+x_{m-1})(a_{m}+x_{m})

in a finite field (G​F​(pn)GF(p^{n})) is Δ\Delta-universal, providing that the keys a1,…,ama_{1},\ldots,a_{m} are picked from all values of the field. In particular, the collision probability between two distinct inputs is bounded by 1/pn1/p^{n}.

4.3 Binary Finite Fields

Finite fields having prime cardinality are simple (see § 4.1), but we would prefer to work with fields having a power-of-two cardinality (also called binary fields) to match common computer architectures. Specifically, we are interested in G​F​(264)GF(2^{64}) because our desktop processors typically have 64-bit architectures.

We can implement such a field over the integers in [0,2L)[0,2^{L}) by using the following two operations. Addition is defined as the bitwise XOR (⊕\oplus) operation, which is fast on most computers:

a+G​F​(2L)b≡a⊕b.\displaystyle a+_{GF(2^{L})}b\equiv a\oplus b.

The number 0 is the additive identity element (a⊕0=0⊕a=aa\oplus 0=0\oplus a=a), and every number is its own additive inverse: a⊕a=0a\oplus a=0. Note that because binary finite fields use XOR as an addition, Δ\Delta-universality and XOR-universality are effectively equivalent for our purposes in binary finite fields.

Multiplication is defined as a carry-less multiplication followed by a reduction. We use the convention that aia_{i} is the ithi^{\mathrm{th}} least significant bit of integer aa and ai=0a_{i}=0 if ii is larger than the most significant bit of aa. The ithi^{\mathrm{th}} bit of the carry-less multiplication a⋆ba\star b of aa and bb is given by

(a⋆b)i≡⨁k=0iai−k​bk\displaystyle(a\star b)_{i}\equiv\bigoplus_{k=0}^{i}a_{i-k}b_{k} (2)

where ai−k​bka_{i-k}b_{k} is just a regular multiplication between two integers in {0,1}\{0,1\} and ⨁k=0i\bigoplus_{k=0}^{i} is the bitwise XOR of a range of values. The carry-less product of two LL-bit integers is a 2​L2L-bit integer. We can check that the integers with ⊕\oplus as addition and ⋆\star as multiplication form a ring: addition and multiplication are associative, commutative and distributive, and there is an additive identity element. In this instance, the number 1 is a multiplicative identity element (a⋆1=1⋆a=aa\star 1=1\star a=a). Except for the number 1, no number has a multiplicative inverse in this ring.

Given the ring determined by ⊕\oplus and ⋆\star, we can derive a corresponding finite field. However, just as with finite fields of prime cardinality, we need some kind of modular reduction and a concept equivalent to that of prime numbers33 3 The general construction of a finite field of cardinality pnp^{n} for n>1n>1 is commonly explained in terms of polynomials with coefficients from G​F​(p)GF(p). To avoid unnecessary abstraction, we present finite fields of cardinality 2L2^{L} using regular LL-bit integers. Interested readers can see Mullen and Panario [30], for the alternative development. .

Let us define degree(x)\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(x) to be the position of the most significant non-zero bit of xx, starting at 0 (e.g., degree(1)=0\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(1)=0, degree(2)=1\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(2)=1, degree(2j)=j\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(2^{j})=j). For example, we have degree(x)≤127\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(x)\leq 127 for any 128-bit integer xx. Given any two non-zero integers a,ba,b, we have that degree(a⋆b)=degree(a)+degree(b)\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(a\star b)=\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(a)+\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(b) as a straightforward consequence of Equation 2. Similarly, we have that

degree(a⊕b)≤max⁡(degree(a),degree(b)).\displaystyle\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(a\oplus b)\leq\max(\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(a),\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(b)).

Not unlike regular multiplication, given integers a,ba,b with b≠0b\neq 0, there are unique integers α,β\alpha,\beta (henceforth the quotient and the remainder) such that

a=α⋆b⊕β\displaystyle a=\alpha\star b\;\oplus\;\beta (3)

where degree(β)<degree(b)\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(\beta)<\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(b).

The uniqueness of the quotient and the remainder is easily shown. Suppose that there is another pair of values α′,β′\alpha^{\prime},\beta^{\prime} with the same property. Then α′⋆b⊕β′=α⋆b⊕β\alpha^{\prime}\star b\;\oplus\;\beta^{\prime}=\alpha\star b\;\oplus\;\beta which implies that (α′⊕α)⋆b=β′⊕β(\alpha^{\prime}\oplus\alpha)\star b=\beta^{\prime}\oplus\beta. However, since degree(β′⊕β)<degree(b)\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(\beta^{\prime}\oplus\beta)<\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(b) we must have that α=α′\alpha=\alpha^{\prime}. From this it follows that β=β′\beta=\beta^{\prime}, thus establishing uniqueness.

We define ÷\div and mod\bmod operators as giving respectively the quotient (a÷b=αa\div b=\alpha) and remainder (amodb=βa\mod b=\beta) so that the equation

a≡a÷b⋆b⊕amodb\displaystyle a\equiv a\div b\star b\;\;\oplus\;\;a\bmod b (4)

is an identity equivalent to Equation 3. (To avoid unnecessary parentheses, we use the following operator precedence convention: ⋆\star, mod\bmod and ÷\div are executed first, from left to right, followed by ⊕\oplus.)

In the general case, we can compute a÷ba\div b and amodba\bmod b using a straightforward variation on the Euclidean division algorithm (see Algorithm 2) which proves the existence of the remainder and quotient. Checking the correctness of the algorithm is straightforward. We start initially with values α\alpha and β\beta such that a=α⋆b⊕βa=\alpha\star b\oplus\beta. By inspection, this equality is preserved throughout the algorithm. Meanwhile, the algorithm only terminates when the degree of β\beta is less than that of bb, as required. And the algorithm must terminate, since the degree of qq is reduced by at least one each time it is updated (for a maximum of degree(a)−degree(b)+1\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(a)-\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(b)+1 steps).

Given a=α⋆b⊕βa=\alpha\star b\;\oplus\;\beta and a′=α′⋆b⊕β′a^{\prime}=\alpha^{\prime}\star b\;\oplus\;\beta^{\prime}, we have that a⊕a′=(α⊕α′)⋆b⊕(β⊕β′)a\oplus a^{\prime}=(\alpha\oplus\alpha^{\prime})\star b\;\oplus\;(\beta\oplus\beta^{\prime}). Thus, it can be checked that divisions and modular reductions are distributive:

(a⊕b)modp=(amodp)⊕(bmodp),\displaystyle(a\oplus b)\bmod p=(a\bmod p)\oplus(b\bmod p), (5)
(a⊕b)÷p=(a÷p)⊕(b÷p).\displaystyle(a\oplus b)\div p=(a\div p)\oplus(b\div p). (6)

Thus, we have (a⊕b)modp=0⇒amodp=bmodp(a\oplus b)\bmod p=0\Rightarrow a\bmod p=b\bmod p. Moreover, by inspection, we have that degree(amodb)<degree(b)\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(a\bmod b)<\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(b) and degree(a÷b)=degree(a)−degree(b)\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(a\div b)=\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(a)-\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(b).

The carry-less multiplication by a power of two is equivalent to regular multiplication. For this reason, a modular reduction by a power of two (e.g., amod264a\bmod{2^{64}}) is just the regular integer modular reduction. Idem for division.

There are non-zero integers aa such that there is no integer bb other than 1 such that amodb=0a\bmod b=0; effectively aa is a prime number under the carry-less multiplication interpretation. These “prime integers” are more commonly known as irreducible polynomials in the ring of polynomials G​F​2​[x]GF2[x], so we call them irreducible instead of prime. Let us pick such an irreducible integer pp (arbitrarily) such that the degree of pp is 64. One such integer is 264+24+23+2+12^{64}+2^{4}+2^{3}+2+1. Then we can finally define the multiplication operation in G​F​(264)GF(2^{64}):

a×G​F​(264)b≡(a⋆b)modp.\displaystyle a\times_{GF(2^{64})}b\equiv(a\star b)\bmod p.

Coupled with the addition +G​F​(264)+_{GF(2^{64})} that is just a bitwise XOR, we have an implementation of the field G​F​(264)GF(2^{64}) over integers in [0,264)[0,2^{64}).

We call the index of the second most significant bit the subdegree. We chose an irreducible pp of degree 64 having minimal subdegree (4).44 4 This can be readily verified using a mathematical software package such as Sage or Maple. We use the fact that this subdegree is small to accelerate the computation of the modular reduction in the next section.

4.4 Efficient Reduction in G​F​(264)GF(2^{64})

AMD and Intel have introduced a fast instruction that can compute a carry-less multiplication between two 64-bit numbers, and it generates a 128-bit integer. To get the multiplication in G​F​(264)GF(2^{64}), we must still reduce this 128-bit integer to a 64-bit integer. Since there is no equivalent fast modular instruction, we need to derive an efficient algorithm.

There are efficient reduction algorithms used in cryptography (e.g., from 256-bit to 128-bit integers [17]), but they do not suit our purposes: we have to reduce to 64-bit integers. Inspired by the classical Barrett reduction [5], Knežević et al. proposed a generic modular reduction algorithm in G​F​(2n)GF(2^{n}), using no more than two multiplications [22]. We put this to good use in previous work [26]. However, we can do the same reduction using a single multiplication. According to our tests, the reduction technique presented next is 30 %30\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} faster than an optimized implementation based on Knežević et al.’s algorithm.

Let us write p=264⊕rp=2^{64}\;\oplus\;r. In our case, we have r=24+23+2+1=27r=2^{4}+2^{3}+2+1=27 and degree(r)=4\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(r)=4. We are interested in applying a modular reduction by pp to the result of the multiplication of two integers in [0,264)[0,2^{64}), and the result of such a multiplication is an integer xx such that degree(x)≤127\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(x)\leq 127. We want to compute xmodpx\bmod p quickly. We begin with the following lemma.

Lemma 6

Consider any 64-bit integer p=264⊕rp=2^{64}\oplus r. We define the operations mod\bmod and ÷\div as the counterparts of the carry-less multiplication ⋆\star as in § 4.3. Given any xx, we have that

xmodp\displaystyle x\bmod p
=((z÷264)⋆264)modp⊕zmod264⊕xmod264\displaystyle=((z\div 2^{64})\star 2^{64})\bmod p\;\oplus\;z\bmod 2^{64}\;\oplus\;x\bmod 2^{64}

where z≡(x÷264)⋆rz\equiv(x\div 2^{64})\star r.

Proof

We have that x=(x÷264)⋆264⊕xmod264x=(x\div 2^{64})\star 2^{64}\;\oplus\;x\bmod 2^{64} for any xx by definition. Applying the modular reduction on both sides of the equality, we get

xmodp\displaystyle x\bmod p =(x÷264)⋆264modp⊕xmod264modp\displaystyle=(x\div 2^{64})\star 2^{64}\bmod p\;\oplus\;x\bmod 2^{64}\bmod p
=(x÷264)⋆264modp⊕xmod264\displaystyle=(x\div 2^{64})\star 2^{64}\bmod p\;\oplus\;x\bmod 2^{64}
by Fact 1
=(x÷264)⋆rmodp⊕xmod264\displaystyle=(x\div 2^{64})\star r\bmod p\;\oplus\;x\bmod 2^{64}
by Fact 2
=zmodp⊕xmod264\displaystyle=z\bmod p\;\oplus\;x\bmod 2^{64}
by z’s def.
=((z÷264)⋆264)modp⊕zmod264\displaystyle=((z\div 2^{64})\star 2^{64})\bmod p\;\oplus\;z\bmod 2^{64}
⊕xmod264\displaystyle\;\oplus\;x\bmod 2^{64}
by Fact 3

where Facts 1, 2 and 3 are as follows:

  • •

    (Fact 1) For any xx, we have that (xmod264)modp=xmod264(x\bmod{2^{64}})\bmod p=x\bmod{2^{64}}.

  • •

    (Fact 2) For any integer zz, we have that (264⊕r)⋆zmodp=p⋆zmodp=0(2^{64}\;\oplus\;r)\star z\bmod p=p\star z\bmod p=0 and therefore

    264⋆zmodp=r⋆zmodp\displaystyle 2^{64}\star z\bmod p=r\star z\bmod p

    by the distributivity of the modular reduction (Equation 5).

  • •

    (Fact 3) Recall that by definition z=(z÷264)⋆264⊕zmod264z=(z\div 2^{64})\star 2^{64}\;\oplus\;z\bmod 2^{64}. We can substitute this equation in the equation from Fact 1. For any zz and any non-zero pp, we have that

    zmodp\displaystyle z\bmod p =((z÷264)⋆264⊕zmod264)modp\displaystyle=((z\div 2^{64})\star 2^{64}\;\oplus\;z\bmod 2^{64})\bmod p
    =((z÷264)⋆264)modp⊕zmod264\displaystyle=((z\div 2^{64})\star 2^{64})\bmod p\;\oplus\;z\bmod 2^{64}

    by the distributivity of the modular reduction (see Equation 5).

Hence the result is shown.

Lemma 6 provides a formula to compute xmodpx\bmod p. Computing z=(x÷264)⋆rz=(x\div 2^{64})\star r involves a carry-less multiplication, which can be done efficiently on recent Intel and AMD processors. The computation of zmod264z\bmod 2^{64} and xmod264x\bmod 2^{64} is trivial. It remains to compute ((z÷264)⋆264)modp((z\div 2^{64})\star 2^{64})\bmod p. At first glance, we still have a modular reduction. However, we can easily memoize the result of ((z÷264)⋆264)modp((z\div 2^{64})\star 2^{64})\bmod p. The next lemma shows that there are only 16 distinct values to memoize (this follows from the low subdegree of pp).

Lemma 7

Given that xx has degree less than 128, there are only 16 possible values of (z÷264)⋆264modp(z\div 2^{64})\star 2^{64}\bmod p, where z≡(x÷264)⋆rz\equiv(x\div 2^{64})\star r and r=24+23+2+1r=2^{4}+2^{3}+2+1.

Proof

Indeed, we have that

degree(z)=degree(x)−64+degree(r).\displaystyle\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(z)=\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(x)-64+\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(r).

Because degree(x)≤127\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(x)\leq 127, we have that degree(z)≤127−64+4=67\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(z)\leq 127-64+4=67. Therefore, we have degree(z÷264)≤3\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(z\div 2^{64})\leq 3. Hence, we can represent z÷264z\div 2^{64} using 4 bits: there are only 16 4-bit integers.

Thus, in the worst possible case, we would need to memoize 16 distinct 128-bit integers to represent ((z÷264)⋆264)modp((z\div 2^{64})\star 2^{64})\bmod p. However, observe that the degree of z÷264z\div 2^{64} is bounded by degree(x)−64+4−64≤127−128+4=3\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(x)-64+4-64\leq 127-128+4=3 since degree(x)≤127\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(x)\leq 127. By using Lemma 8, we show that each integer ((z÷264)⋆264)modp((z\div 2^{64})\star 2^{64})\bmod p has degree bounded by 7 so that it can be represented using no more than 8 bits: setting L=64L=64 and w≡z÷264w\equiv z\div 2^{64}, degree(w)≤3\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(w)\leq 3, degree(r)=4\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(r)=4 and degree(w)+degree(r)≤7\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(w)+\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(r)\leq 7.

Effectively, the lemma says that if you take a value of small degree ww, you multiply it by 2L2^{{L}} and then compute the modular reduction on the result and a value pp that is almost 2L2^{L} (except for a value of small degree rr), then the result has small degree: it is bounded by the sum of the degrees of ww and rr.

Lemma 8

Consider p=2L⊕rp=2^{L}\;\oplus\;r, with rr of degree less than LL. For any ww, the degree of w⋆2Lmodpw\star 2^{L}\bmod p is bounded by degree(w)+degree(r)\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(w)+\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(r).

Moreover, when degree(w)+degree(r)<L\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(w)+\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(r)<L then the degree of w⋆2Lmodpw\star 2^{L}\bmod p is exactly degree(w)+degree(r)\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(w)+\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(r).

Proof

The result is trivial if degree(w)+degree(r)≥L\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(w)+\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(r)\geq L, since the degree of w⋆2Lmodpw\star 2^{L}\bmod p must be smaller than the degree of pp.

So let us assume that degree(w)+degree(r)<L\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(w)+\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(r)<L. By the definition of the modular reduction (Equation 4), we have

w⋆2L\displaystyle w\star 2^{L} =w⋆2L÷p⋆p⊕w⋆2Lmodp.\displaystyle=w\star 2^{L}\div p\star p\;\;\oplus\;\;w\star 2^{L}\bmod p.

Let w′=w⋆2L÷pw^{\prime}=w\star 2^{L}\div p, then

w⋆2L\displaystyle w\star 2^{L} =w′⋆p⊕w⋆2Lmodp\displaystyle=w^{\prime}\star p\;\;\oplus\;\;w\star 2^{L}\bmod p
=w′⋆r⊕w′⋆2L⊕w⋆2Lmodp.\displaystyle=w^{\prime}\star r\;\;\oplus\;\;w^{\prime}\star 2^{L}\;\;\oplus\;\;w\star 2^{L}\bmod p.

The first LL bits of w⋆2Lw\star 2^{L} and w′⋆2Lw^{\prime}\star 2^{L} are zero. Therefore, we have

(w′⋆r)mod2L\displaystyle(w^{\prime}\star r)\bmod 2^{L} =(w⋆2Lmodp)mod2L.\displaystyle=(w\star 2^{L}\bmod p)\bmod 2^{L}.

Moreover, the degree of w′w^{\prime} is the same as the degree of ww: degree(w′)=degree(w)+degree(2L)+degree(p)=degree(w)+L−L=degree(w)\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(w^{\prime})=\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(w)+\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(2^{L})+\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(p)=\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(w)+L-L=\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(w). Hence, we have degree(w′⋆r)=degree(w)+degree(r)<L\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(w^{\prime}\star r)=\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(w)+\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(r)<L. And, of course, degree(w⋆2Lmodp)<L\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(w\star 2^{L}\bmod p)<L. Thus, we have that

w′⋆r=w⋆2Lmodp.\displaystyle w^{\prime}\star r=w\star 2^{L}\bmod p.

Hence, it follows that degree(w⋆2Lmodp)=degree(w′⋆r)=degree(w)+degree(r)\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(w\star 2^{L}\bmod p)=\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(w^{\prime}\star r)=\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(w)+\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(r).

Thus the memoization requires access to only 16 8-bit values. We enumerate the values in question (w⋆264modpw\star 2^{64}\bmod p for w=0,1,…,15w=0,1,\ldots,15) in Table 3. It is convenient that 16×8=12816\times 8=128 bits: the entire table fits in a 128-bit word. It means that if the list of 8-bit values are stored using one byte each, the SSSE3 instruction pshufb can be used for fast look-up. (See Algorithm 3.)

5 CLHASH

The CLHASH family resembles the VHASH family — except that members work in a binary finite field. The VHASH family has the 128-bit NH family (see Equation 1), but we instead use the 128-bit CLNH family:

CLNH⁡(s)=⨁i=1l/2((s2​i−1⊕k2​i−1)⋆(s2​i⊕k2​i))\mathrm{CLNH}(s)=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{l/2}\big((s_{2i-1}\oplus k_{2i-1})\star(s_{2i}\oplus k_{2i})\big) (7)

where the sis_{i} and kik_{i}’s are 64-bit integers and ll is the length of the string ss. The formula assumes that ll is even: we pad odd-length inputs with a single zero word. When an input string MM is made of |M||M| bytes, we can consider it as string of 64-bit words ss by padding it with up to 7 zero bytes so that |M||M| is divisible by 8.

On x64 processors with the CLMUL instruction set, a single term ((s2​i−1⊕k2​i−1)⋆(s2​i⊕k2​i))((s_{2i-1}\oplus k_{2i-1})\star(s_{2i}\oplus k_{2i})) can be computed using one 128-bit XOR instructions (pxor in SSE2) and one carry-less multiplication using the pclmulqdq instruction:

  • •

    load (k2​i−1,k2​i)(k_{2i-1},k_{2i}) in a 128-bit word,

  • •

    load (s2​i−1,s2​i)(s_{2i-1},s_{2i}) in another 128-bit word,

  • •

    compute

    (k2​i−1,k2​i)⊕(s2​i−1,s2​i)≡(k2​i−1⊕s2​i−1,k2​i⊕s2​i)\displaystyle(k_{2i-1},k_{2i})\oplus(s_{2i-1},s_{2i})\equiv(k_{2i-1}\oplus s_{2i-1},k_{2i}\oplus s_{2i})

    using one pxor instruction,

  • •

    compute (k2​i−1⊕s2​i−1)⋆(k2​i⊕s2​i)(k_{2i-1}\oplus s_{2i-1})\star(k_{2i}\oplus s_{2i}) using one pclmulqdq instruction (result is a 128-bit word).

An additional pxor instruction is required per pair of words to compute CLNH, since we need to aggregate the results.

We have that the family s→CLNH⁡(s)modps\to\mathrm{CLNH}(s)\bmod p for some irreducible pp of degree 64 is XOR universal over same-length strings. Indeed, Δ\Delta-universality in the field G​F​(264)GF(2^{64}) follows from Lemma 5. However, recall that Δ\Delta-universality in a binary finite field (with operations ⋆\star and ⊕\oplus for multiplication and addition) is the same as XOR universality — addition is the XOR operation (⊕\oplus). It follows that the CLNH family must be 1/2641/2^{64}-almost universal for same-length strings.

Given an arbitrarily long string of 64-bit words, we can divide it up into blocks of 128 words (padding the last block with zeros if needed). Each block can be hashed using CLNH and the result is 1/2641/2^{64}-almost universal by Lemma 2. If there is a single block, we can compute CLNH⁡(s)modp\mathrm{CLNH}(s)\bmod p to get an XOR universal hash value. Otherwise, the resulting 128-bit hash values a1,a2,…,ana_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{n} can then be hashed once more. For this we use a polynomial hash function, kn−1​a1+kn−2​a2+⋯+ank^{n-1}a_{1}+k^{n-2}a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}, for some random input kk in some finite field. We choose the field G​F​(2127)GF(2^{127}) and use the irreducible p=2127+2+1p=2^{127}+2+1. We compute such a polynomial hash function by using Horner’s rule: starting with r=a1r=a_{1}, compute r←k⋆r⊕air\leftarrow k\star r\oplus a_{i} for i=2,3,…,ni=2,3,\ldots,n. For this purpose, we need carry-less multiplications between pairs of 128-bit integers: we can achieve the desired result with 4 pclmulqdq instructions, in addition to some shift and XOR operations. The multiplication generates a 256-bit integer xx that must be reduced. However, it is not necessary to reduce it to a 127-bit integer (which would be the result if we applied a modular reduction by 2127+2+12^{127}+2+1). It is enough to reduce it to a 128-bit integer x′x^{\prime} such that x′mod(2127+2+1)=xmod(2127+2+1)x^{\prime}\bmod(2^{127}+2+1)=x\bmod(2^{127}+2+1). We get the desired result by setting x′x^{\prime} equal to the lazy modular reduction [8] xmodlazy(2127+2+1)x\bmod_{\mathrm{lazy}}(2^{127}+2+1) defined as

\displaystyle xmodlazy(2127+2+1)\displaystyle x\bmod_{\mathrm{lazy}}(2^{127}+2+1) (8)
≡xmod((2127+2+1)⋆2)\displaystyle\equiv x\bmod((2^{127}+2+1)\star 2)
=xmod(2128+4+2)\displaystyle=x\bmod(2^{128}+4+2)
=(xmod2128)⊕((x÷2128)⋆4⊕(x÷2128)⋆2).\displaystyle=(x\bmod 2^{128})\oplus((x\div 2^{128})\star 4\oplus(x\div 2^{128})\star 2).

It is computationally convenient to assume that degree(x)≤256−2\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(x)\leq 256-2 so that degree((x÷2128)⋆4)≤128\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}((x\div 2^{128})\star 4)\leq 128. We can achieve this degree bound by picking the polynomial coefficient kk to have degree(k)≤128−2\mathop{\mathrm{degree}}(k)\leq 128-2. The resulting polynomial hash family is (n−1)/2126(n-1)/2^{126}-almost universal for strings having the same length where nn is the number of 128-word blocks (⌈|M|/1024⌉\lceil|M|/1024\rceil where |M||M| is the string length in bytes), whether we use the actual modular or the lazy modular reduction.

It remains to reduce the final output 𝒪\mathcal{O} (stored in a 128-bit word) to a 64-bit hash value. For this purpose, we can use s→CLNH⁡(s)modps\to\mathrm{CLNH}(s)\bmod p with p=264+27p=2^{64}+27 (see § 4.4), and where k′′k^{\prime\prime} is a random 64-bit integer. We treat 𝒪\mathcal{O} as a string containing two 64-bit words. Once more, the reduction is XOR universal by an application of Lemma 5. Thus, we have the composition of three hash functions with collision probabilities 1/2641/2^{64}, (n−1)/2126(n-1)/2^{126} and 1/2641/2^{64}. It is reasonable to bound the string length by 2642^{64} bytes: n≤264/1024=254n\leq 2^{64}/1024=2^{54}. We have that 2/264+(254−1)/2126<2.004/2642/2^{64}+(2^{54}-1)/2^{126}<2.004/2^{64}. Thus, for same-length strings, we have 2.004/2642.004/2^{64}-almost XOR universality.

We further ensure that the result is XOR-universal over all strings: P⁡(h⁡(s)=h⁡(s′)⊕c)≤1/264P\left(h(s)=h(s^{\prime})\oplus c\right)\leq 1/2^{64} irrespective of whether |s|=|s′||s|=|s^{\prime}|. By Lemma 3, it suffices to XOR the hash value with k′′⋆|M|modpk^{\prime\prime}\star|M|\bmod p where k′′k^{\prime\prime} is a random 64-bit integer and |M||M| is the string length as a 64-bit integer, and where p=264+27p=2^{64}+27. The XOR universality follows for strings having different lengths by Lemma 4 and the equivalence between XOR-universality and Δ\Delta-universality in binary finite fields. As a practical matter, since the final step involves the same modular reduction twice in the expression (CLNH⁡(s)modp)⊕((k′′⋆|M|)modp)(\mathrm{CLNH}(s)\bmod p)\oplus((k^{\prime\prime}\star|M|)\bmod p), we can simplify it to (CLNH⁡(s)⊕(k′′⋆|M|))modp(\mathrm{CLNH}(s)\oplus(k^{\prime\prime}\star|M|))\bmod p, thus avoiding an unnecessary modular reduction.

Our analysis is summarized by following lemma.

Lemma 9

CLHASH is 2.004/2642.004/2^{64}-almost XOR universal over strings of up to 2642^{64} bytes. Moreover, it is XOR universal over strings of no more than 1 kB1\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{B}.

The bound of the collision probability of CLHASH for long strings (2.004/2642.004/2^{64}) is 4 times lower than the corresponding VHASH collision probability (1/2611/2^{61}). For short strings (1 kB1\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{B} or less), CLHASH has a bound that is 8 times lower. See Table 4 for a comparison. CLHASH is given by Algorithm 4.

5.1 Random Bits

One might wonder whether using 1 kB1\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{B} of random bits is necessary. For strings of no more than 1 kB1\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{B}, CLHASH is XOR universal. Stinson showed that in such cases, we need the number of random bits to match the input length [37]. That is, we need at least 1 kB1\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{B} to achieve XOR universality over strings having 1 kB1\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{B}. Hence, CLHASH makes nearly optimal use of the random bits.

6 Statistical Validation

Classically, hash functions have been deterministic: fixed maps hh from UU to VV, where |U|≫|V||U|\gg|V| and thus collisions are inevitable. Hash functions might be assessed according to whether their outputs are distributed evenly, i.e., whether |h−1​(x)|≈|h−1​(y)||h^{-1}(x)|\approx|h^{-1}(y)| for two distinct x,y∈Vx,y\in V. However, in practice, the actual input is likely to consist of clusters of nearly identical keys [23]: for instance, symbol table entries such as temp1, temp2, temp3 are to be expected, or a collection of measured data values is likely to contain clusters of similar numeric values. Appending an extra character to the end of an input string, or flipping a bit in an input number, should (usually) result in a different hash value. A collection of desirable properties can be defined, and then hash functions rated on their performance on data that is meant to represent realistic cases.

One common use of randomized hashing is to avoid DoS (denial-of-service) attacks when an adversary controls the series of keys submitted to a hash table. In this setting, prior to the use of a hash table, a random selection of hash function is made from the family. The (deterministic) function is then used, at least until the number of collisions is observed to be too high. A high number of collisions presumably indicates the hash table needs to be resized, although it could indicate that an undesirable member of the family had been chosen. Those contemplating switching from deterministic hash tables to randomized hash tables would like to know that typical performance would not degrade much. Yet, as carefully tuned deterministic functions can sometimes outperform random assignments for typical inputs [23], some degradation might need to be tolerated. Thus, it is worth checking a few randomly chosen members of our CLHASH families against statistical tests.

6.1 SMHasher

The SMHasher program [1] includes a variety of quality tests on a number of minimally randomized hashing algorithms, for which we have weak or no known theoretical guarantees. It runs several statistical tests, such as the following.

  • •

    Given a randomly generated input, changing a few bits at random should not generate a collision.

  • •

    Among all inputs containing only two non-zero bytes (and having a fixed length in [4,20][4,20]), collisions should be unlikely (called the TwoBytes test).

  • •

    Changing a single bit in the input should change half the bits of the hash value, on average [13] (sometimes called the avalanche effect).

Some of these tests are demanding: e.g., CityHash [35] fails the TwoBytes test.

We added both VHASH and CLHASH to SMHasher and used the Mersenne Twister (i.e., MT19937) to generate the random bits [28]. We find that VHASH passes all tests. However, CLHASH fails one of them: the avalanche test. We can illustrate the failure. Consider that for short fixed-length strings (8 bytes or less), CLHASH is effectively equivalent to a hash function of the form h⁡(x)=a⋆xmodph(x)=a\star x\bmod p, where pp is irreducible. Such hash functions form an XOR universal family. They also satisfy the identity h⁡(x⊕y)⊕h⁡(x)=h⁡(y)h(x\oplus y)\oplus h(x)=h(y). It follows that no matter what value xx takes, modifying the same ithi^{\mathrm{th}} bit modifies the resulting hash value in a consistent manner (according to h⁡(2i+1)h(2^{i+1})). We can still expect that changing a bit in the input changes half the bits of the hash value on average. However, SMHasher checks that h⁡(x⊕2i+1)h(x\oplus 2^{i+1}) differs from h⁡(x)h(x) in any given bit about half the time over many randomly chosen inputs xx. Since h⁡(x⊕2i+1)⊕h⁡(x)h(x\oplus 2^{i+1})\oplus h(x) is independent from xx for short inputs with CLHASH, any given bit is either always flipped (for all xx) or never. Hence, CLHASH fails the SMHasher test.

Thankfully, we can slightly modify CLHASH so that all tests pass if we so desire. It suffices to apply an additional bit mixing function taken from MurmurHash [1] to the result of CLHASH. The function consists of two multiplications and three shifts over 64-bit integers:

x\displaystyle x ←x⊕(x≫33),\displaystyle\leftarrow x\oplus(x\gg 33),
x\displaystyle x ←x×18397679294719823053,\displaystyle\leftarrow x\times 18397679294719823053,
x\displaystyle x ←x⊕(x≫33),\displaystyle\leftarrow x\oplus(x\gg 33),
x\displaystyle x ←x×14181476777654086739,\displaystyle\leftarrow x\times 14181476777654086739,
x\displaystyle x ←x⊕(x≫33).\displaystyle\leftarrow x\oplus(x\gg 33).

Each step is a bijection: e.g., multiplication by an odd integer is always invertible. A bijection does not affect collision bounds.

7 Speed Experiments

We implemented a performance benchmark in C and compiled our software using GNU GCC 4.8 with the -O2 flag. The benchmark program ran on a Linux server with an Intel i7-4770 processor running at 3.4 GHz3.4\text{\,}\mathrm{G}\mathrm{H}\mathrm{z}. This CPU has 32 kB32\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{B} of L1 cache, 256 kB256\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{B} of L2 cache per core, and 8 MB8\text{\,}\mathrm{M}\mathrm{B} of L3 cache shared by all cores. The machine has 32 GB32\text{\,}\mathrm{G}\mathrm{B} of RAM (DDR3-1600 with double-channel). We disabled Turbo Boost and set the processor to run only at its highest clock speed, effectively disabling the processor’s power management. All timings are done using the time-stamp counter (rdtsc) instruction [34]. Although all our software55 5 Our benchmark software is made freely available under a liberal open-source license (https://github.com/lemire/StronglyUniversalStringHashing), and it includes the modified SMHasher as well as all the necessary software to reproduce our results. is single-threaded, we disabled hyper-threading as well.

Our experiments compare implementations of CLHASH, VHASH, SipHash [3], GHASH [17] and Google’s CityHash.

  • •

    We implemented CLHASH using Intel intrinsics. As described in § 5, we use various single instruction, multiple data (SIMD) instructions (e.g., SSE2, SSE3 and SSSE3) in addition to the CLMUL instruction set. The random bits are stored consecutively in memory, aligned with a cache line (64 bytes).

  • •

    For VHASH, we used the authors’ 64-bit implementation [25], which is optimized with inline assembly. It stores the random bits in a C struct, and we do not include the overhead of constructing this struct in the timings. The authors assume that the input length is divisible by 16 bytes, or padded with zeros to the nearest 16-byte boundary. In some instances, we would need to copy part of the input to a new location prior to hashing the content to satisfy the requirement. Instead, we decided to optimistically hash the data in-place without copy. Thus, we slightly overestimate the speed of the VHASH implementation — especially on shorter strings.

  • •

    We used the reference C implementation of SipHash [4]. SipHash is a fast family of 64-bit pseudorandom hash functions adopted, among others, by the Python language.

  • •

    CityHash is commonly used in applications where high speed is desirable [27, 15]. We wrote a simple C port of Google’s CityHash (version 1.1.1) [35]. Specifically, we benchmarked the CityHash64WithSeed function.

  • •

    Using Gueron and Kounavis’ [17] code, we implemented a fast version of GHASH accelerated with the CLMUL instruction set. GHASH is a polynomial hash function over G​F​(2128)GF(2^{128}) using the irreducible polynomial x128+x7+x2+x+1x^{128}+x^{7}+x^{2}+x+1: h⁡(x1,x2,…,xn)=an​x1+an−1​x2+…+a​xnh(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})=a^{n}x_{1}+a^{n-1}x_{2}+\ldots+ax_{n} for some 128-bit key aa. To accelerate computations, Gueron and Kounavis replace the traditional Horner’s rule with an extended version that processes input words four at a time: starting with r=0r=0 and precomputed powers a2,a3,a4a^{2},a^{3},a^{4}, compute r←a4​(r+xi)+a3​xi+1+a2​xi+2+a​xi+3r\leftarrow a^{4}(r+x_{i})+a^{3}x_{i+1}+a^{2}x_{i+2}+ax_{i+3} for i=1,4,…,4​⌊m/4⌋−3i=1,4,\ldots,4\lfloor m/4\rfloor-3. We complete the computation with the usual Horner’s rule when the number of input words is not divisible by four. In contrast with other hash functions, GHASH generates 128-bit hash values.

VHASH, CLHASH and GHASH require random bits. The time spent by the random-number generator is excluded from the timings.

7.1 Results

We find that the hashing speed is not sensitive to the content of the inputs — thus we generated the inputs using a random-number generator. For any given input length, we repeatly hash the strings so that, in total, 40 million input words have been processed.

As a first test, we hashed 64 B64\text{\,}\mathrm{B} and 4 kB4\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{B} inputs (see Table 5) and we report the number of cycles spent to hash one byte: for 4 kB4\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{B} inputs, we got 0.26 for VHASH,66 6 For comparison, Dai and Krovetz reported that VHASH used 0.6 cycles per byte on an Intel Core 2 processor (Merom) [25]. 0.16 for CLHASH, 0.23 for CityHash and 0.93 for GHASH. That is, CLHASH is over 60 %60\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} faster than VHASH and almost 45 %45\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} faster than CityHash. Moreover, SipHash is an order of magnitude slower. Considering that it produces 128-bit hash values, the PCMUL-accelerated GHASH offers good performance: it uses less than one cycle per input byte for long inputs.

Of course, the relative speeds depend on the length of the input. In Fig. 1, we vary the input length from 8 bytes to 8 kB8\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{B}. We see that the results for input lengths of 4 kB4\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{B} are representative. Mostly, we have that CLHASH is 60 %60\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} faster than VHASH and 40 %40\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} faster than CityHash. However, CityHash and CLHASH have similar performance for small inputs (32 bytes or less) whereas VHASH fares poorly over these same small inputs. We find that SipHash is not competitive in these tests.

7.2 Analysis

From an algorithmic point of view, VHASH and CLHASH are similar. Moreover, VHASH uses a conventional multiplication operation that has lower latency and higher throughput than CLHASH. And the VHASH implementation relies on hand-tuned assembly code. Yet CLHASH is 60 %60\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} faster.

For long strings, the bulk of the VHASH computation is spent computing the NH function. When computing NH, each pair of input words (or 16 bytes) uses the following instructions: one mulq, three adds and one adc. Both mulq and adc generate two micro-operations (μ\muops) each, so without counting register loading operations, we need at least 3+2×2=73+2\times 2=7 μ\muops to process two words [16]. Yet Haswell processors, like other recent Intel processors, are apparently limited to a sustained execution of no more than per cycle. Thus we need at least 7/47/4 cycles for every 16 bytes. That is, VHASH needs at least 0.11 cycles per byte. Because CLHASH runs at 0.16 cycles per byte on long strings (see Table 5), we have that no implementation of VHASH could surpass our implementation of CLHASH by more than 35 %35\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}. Simply put, VHASH requires too many μ\muops.

CLHASH is not similarly limited. For each pair of input 64-bit words, CLNH uses two 128-bit XOR instructions (pxor) and one pclmulqdq instruction. Each pxor uses one (fused) μ\muop whereas the pclmulqdq instruction uses two μ\muops for a total of , versus the absolutely needed by VHASH. Thus, the number of μ\muops dispatched per cycle is less likely to be a bottleneck for CLHASH. However, the pclmulqdq instruction has a throughput of only two cycles per instruction. Thus, we can only process one pair of 64-bit words every two cycles, for a speed of 2/16=0.1252/16=0.125 cycles per byte. The measured speed (0.16 cycles per byte) is about 35 %35\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} higher than this lower bound according to Table 5. This suggests that our implementation of CLHASH is nearly optimal — at least for long strings. We verified our analysis with the IACA code analyser [19]. It reports that VHASH is indeed limited by the number of μ\muops that can be dispatched per cycle, unlike CLHASH.

8 Related Work

The work that lead to the design of the pclmulqdq instruction by Gueron and Kounavis [17] introduced efficient algorithms using this instruction, e.g., an algorithm for 128-bit modular reduction in Galois Counter Mode. Since then, the pclmulqdq instruction has been used to speed up cryptographic applications. Su and Fan find that the Karatsuba formula becomes especially efficient for software implementations of multiplication in binary finite fields due to the pclmulqdq instruction [38]. Bos et al. [9] used the CLMUL instruction set for 256-bit hash functions on the Westmere microarchitecture. Elliptic curve cryptography benefits from the pclmulqdq instruction [32, 33, 39]. Bluhm and Gueron pointed out that the benefits are increased on the Haswell microarchitecture due to the higher throughput and lower latency of the instruction [8].

In previous work, we used the pclmulqdq instruction for fast 32-bit random hashing on the Sandy Bridge and Bulldozer architectures [26]. However, our results were disappointing, due in part to the low throughput of the instruction on these older microarchitectures.

9 Conclusion

The pclmulqdq instruction on recent Intel processors enables a fast and almost universal 64-bit hashing family (CLHASH). In terms of raw speed, the hash functions from this family can surpass some of the fastest 64-bit hash functions on x64 processors (VHASH and CityHash). Moreover, CLHASH offers superior bounds on the collision probability. CLHASH makes optimal use of the random bits, in the sense that it offers XOR universality for short strings (less than 1 kB1\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{B}).

We believe that CLHASH might be suitable for many common purposes. The VHASH family has been proposed for cryptographic applications, and specifically message authentication (VMAC): similar applications are possible for CLHASH. Future work should investigate these applications.

Other microprocessor architectures also support fast carry-less multiplication, sometimes referring to it as polynomial multiplication (e.g., ARM [2] and Power [20]). Future work might review the performance of CLHASH on these architectures. It might also consider the acceleration of alternative hash families such as those based on Toeplitz matrices [37].
